modern_osis:
Colossians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

This letter was sent because difficulties had arisen among the Colossians, probably through the influence of false teachers. Those difficulties led them to seek Paul's guidance.

The letter's purpose is to show that all hope of human redemption rests on Jesus Christ, in whom alone are complete fullness, perfection and sufficiency.

Paul warned the Colossians against both teachers who wanted to impose Jewish observances and notions arising from worldly wisdom, human inventions and traditions. All of these could undermine complete dependence upon Christ.

The first two chapters teach the beliefs Christians must hold. The last two chapters teach the conduct those beliefs require: the doctrine of faith and the duties of Christian life for salvation.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle Paul salutes the Colossians, and blesses God for their faith, love, and hope.1–8Prays for their fruitfulness in spiritual knowledge.9–14Gives a glorious view of Christ.15–23And sets out his own character, as the apostle of the Gentiles.24–29
Faith, hope and love grow from the gospel (verses 1–8)

All genuine Christians are brothers and sisters in Christ.

Faithfulness should mark every Christian role and relationship.

Faith, hope and love are the three great graces of the Christian life, and we have reason to bring each of them before God in prayer and thanksgiving.

When we place our hope firmly in the reward God has prepared in the life to come, we become more willing to use earthly resources for the good of others.

The heavenly inheritance is safely stored for believers; no enemy can take it away.

The gospel is God's true word, and we can safely entrust our souls to its promises.

Those who hear the gospel should also bear its fruit.

They ought to obey it, allowing it to shape their convictions, principles and conduct.

Worldly affection often arises from advantage or similarity in habits. Carnal affection seeks pleasure.

Both forms of affection are easily mixed with selfishness and other corrupt motives.

But Christian love is born of the Holy Spirit and is marked by holiness.

Paul's prayer for knowledge, strength and endurance (verses 9–14)

Paul prayed continually that the believers would be filled with knowledge of God's will and spiritual wisdom.

Good words are not enough without good works.

The God who gives his people strength possesses glorious power, and the blessed Holy Spirit is the source of this work within them.

God's promises are abundant. We need not restrict our prayers or hopes for spiritual strength as though he lacked resources to provide it.

God's grace in the believer's heart is his power, a power full of glory.

A special purpose of this strength is to sustain us during suffering.

There remains work to be done even when we are afflicted.

Amid trials, believers can give thanks to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose special grace prepares them to share in the inheritance of the saints.

Those once enslaved by Satan become willing subjects of Jesus Christ.

Everyone destined for heaven must be prepared for heaven while still here.

Those who receive the inheritance of God's children must also receive the training and character of his children.

Through faith in Christ, they enjoy redemption, purchased through his atoning blood, and thus receive forgiveness of sins and every spiritual blessing.

What mercy to be delivered from Satan's kingdom and brought into the kingdom of Christ!

All present suffering will eventually end, and every believer will be among those who come through great tribulation into glory.

Christ creates, sustains and reconciles all things (verses 15–23)

In his human nature, Christ makes the invisible God visible.

Whoever has seen Christ has seen the Father.

We should contemplate these mysteries with humble faith, recognizing God's glory in Jesus Christ.

Scripture describes the Son as born or begotten before any creature existed, representing his eternity in language we can understand.

All things were created through him and for him.

His power brought them into existence.

They exist according to his will and for his praise and glory.

He also sustains everything by his powerful word.

As Mediator, Christ is the Head of the church, which is his body.

All its grace, strength and life come from him.

All fullness dwells in Christ: fullness of merit and righteousness, strength and grace sufficient for all who believe.

God displayed his justice by requiring complete satisfaction for sin.

Christ's death was the fitting means through which sinners could be redeemed and reconciled to their Maker.

Though God hates sin, he was pleased to reconcile fallen human beings to himself through Jesus Christ.

We were formerly enemies in our minds, displaying hostility through wicked actions.

Yet through Christ's sacrifice and death in our human nature, we can be reconciled.

We should neither explain away these mysteries nor imagine that our limited minds can comprehend them completely.

Rather, we should behold the beauty of this plan of salvation and rejoice in the hope it gives.

If God has shown such extraordinary love toward us, how should we respond?

Be constant in prayer and diligent in holy service.

Do not continue living for yourself.

Christ died for us not so that we would persist in sin, but so that we would die to sin and live for him.

Paul serves Christ's church through suffering (verses 24–29)

The sufferings of Christ the Head and of his church as the members of his body are spoken of together.

Yet their purposes are not the same.

Christ suffered to redeem his church. His people suffer for other reasons.

The afflictions we endure are a small share compared with the bitter cup he drank for us.

A Christian can be said to complete what remains of Christ's sufferings when that person takes up the cross, follows his example and patiently bears the trials God assigns.

Let us thank God for revealing mysteries hidden through many generations and for making known the riches of his glory among us.

Since Christ is preached among us, we should ask seriously: Does he truly live and reign within us?

Only Christ's indwelling provides a firm ground for the hope of his glory.

We must remain faithful even to death, enduring every trial, so that we may receive the crown of life and reach the final purpose of our faith—the salvation of our souls.
classic_reading:
[Col.1.1-Col.1.8]
Colossians
This epistle was sent because of some difficulties which arose among the Colossians, probably from false teachers, in consequence of which they sent to the apostle. The scope of the epistle is to show, that all hope of man's redemption is founded on Christ, in whom alone are all complete fulness, perfections, and sufficiency. The Colossians are cautioned against the devices of judaizing teachers, and also against the notions of carnal wisdom, and human inventions and traditions, as not consistent with full reliance on Christ. In the first two chapters the apostle tells them what they must believe, and in the two last what they must do; the doctrine of faith, and the precepts of life for salvation.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
The apostle Paul salutes the Colossians, and blesses God for their faith, love, and hope. | (1-8) |
Prays for their fruitfulness in spiritual knowledge. | (9-14) |
Gives a glorious view of Christ. | (15-23) |
And sets out his own character, as the apostle of the Gentiles. | (24-29) |
Verses 1-8
All true Christians are brethren one to another. Faithfulness runs through every character and relation of the Christian life. Faith, hope, and love, are the three principal graces in the Christian life, and proper matter for prayer and thanksgiving. The more we fix our hopes on the reward in the other world, the more free shall we be in doing good with our earthly treasure. It was treasured up for them, no enemy could deprive them of it. The gospel is the word of truth, and we may safely venture our souls upon it. And all who hear the word of the gospel, ought to bring forth the fruit of the gospel, obey it, and have their principles and lives formed according to it. Worldly love arises, either from views of interest or from likeness in manners; carnal love, from the appetite for pleasure. To these, something corrupt, selfish, and base always cleaves. But Christian love arises from the Holy Spirit, and is full of holiness. ( [Col.1.9-Col.1.14] Col 1:9-14)
[Col.1.9-Col.1.14]
Verses 9-14
The apostle was constant in prayer, that the believers might be filled with the knowledge of God's will, in all wisdom. Good words will not do without good works. He who undertakes to give strength to his people, is a God of power, and of glorious power. The blessed Spirit is the author of this. In praying for spiritual strength, we are not straitened, or confined in the promises, and should not be so in our hopes and desires. The grace of God in the hearts of believers is the power of God; and there is glory in this power. The special use of this strength was for sufferings. There is work to be done, even when we are suffering. Amidst all their trials they gave thanks to the Father of our Lord Jesus, whose special grace fitted them to partake of the inheritance provided for the saints. To bring about this change, those were made willing subjects of Christ, who were slaves of Satan. All who are designed for heaven hereafter, are prepared for heaven now. Those who have the inheritance of sons, have the education of sons, and the disposition of sons. By faith in Christ they enjoyed this redemption, as the purchase of his atoning blood, whereby forgiveness of sins, and all other spiritual blessings were bestowed. Surely then we shall deem it a favour to be delivered from Satan's kingdom and brought into that of Christ, knowing that all trials will soon end, and that every believer will be found among those who come out of great tribulation.
[Col.1.15-Col.1.23]
Verses 15-23
Christ in his human nature, is the visible discovery of the invisible God, and he that hath seen Him hath seen the Father. Let us adore these mysteries in humble faith, and behold the glory of the Lord in Christ Jesus. He was born or begotten before all the creation, before any creature was made; which is the Scripture way of representing eternity, and by which the eternity of God is represented to us. All things being created by Him, were created for him; being made by his power, they were made according to his pleasure, and for his praise and glory. He not only created them all at first, but it is by the word of his power that they are upheld. Christ as Mediator is the Head of the body, the church; all grace and strength are from him; and the church is his body. All fulness dwells in him; a fulness of merit and righteousness, of strength and grace for us. God showed his justice in requiring full satisfaction. This mode of redeeming mankind by the death of Christ was most suitable. Here is presented to our view the method of being reconciled. And that, notwithstanding the hatred of sin on God's part, it pleased God to reconcile fallen man to himself. If convinced that we were enemies in our minds by wicked works, and that we are now reconciled to God by the sacrifice and death of Christ in our nature, we shall not attempt to explain away, nor yet think fully to comprehend these mysteries; but we shall see the glory of this plan of redemption, and rejoice in the hope set before us. If this be so, that God's love is so great to us, what shall we do now for God? Be frequent in prayer, and abound in holy duties; and live no more to yourselves, but to Christ. Christ died for us. But wherefore? That we should still live in sin? No; but that we should die to sin, and live henceforth not to ourselves, but to Him.
[Col.1.24-Col.1.29]
Verses 24-29
Both the sufferings of the Head and of the members are called the sufferings of Christ, and make up, as it were, one body of sufferings. But He suffered for the redemption of the church; we suffer on other accounts; for we do but slightly taste that cup of afflictions of which Christ first drank deeply. A Christian may be said to fill up that which remains of the sufferings of Christ, when he takes up his cross, and after the pattern of Christ, bears patiently the afflictions God allots to him. Let us be thankful that God has made known to us mysteries hidden from ages and generations, and has showed the riches of his glory among us. As Christ is preached among us, let us seriously inquire, whether he dwells and reigns in us; for this alone can warrant our assured hope of his glory. We must be faithful to death, through all trials, that we may receive the crown of life, and obtain the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle expresses his love to, and joy in believers.1–7He cautions against the errors of heathen philosophy; also against Jewish traditions, and rites which had been fulfilled in Christ.8–17Against worshipping angels; and against legal ordinances.18–23
Christ contains the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (verses 1–7)

Our souls prosper when we acquire clear knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus.

That truth should be believed in the heart and confessed openly when circumstances call for it.

Knowledge and genuine faith make a soul rich.

The stronger our faith and the warmer our love, the greater comfort we receive.

The treasures of wisdom are hidden in Christ not to keep them from us, but to preserve them for us.

They remain hidden from proud unbelievers, yet are displayed in Christ's person and saving work.

Beware of persuasive but misleading words.

Evil ideas and practices often appear attractive through clever disguises.

People who try to draw us into wickedness aim to rob us of what is precious.

Every professing Christian claims to have received Jesus Christ as Lord, agreeing to belong to him.

But we cannot grow in Christ until we are first rooted in him and founded upon him.

Having been established in faith, we should continue increasing in it and developing its fruits.

Thanksgiving must accompany this growth.

God justly withholds some blessings when people receive his gifts without grateful hearts.

Complete in Christ, not in religious shadows (verses 8–17)

There is a form of philosophy that rightly exercises our minds.

By studying God's works in creation, it leads us toward knowledge of him and confirms faith.

But there is another kind of philosophy that is empty and deceptive, entertaining human imagination while undermining belief.

It involves speculative questions beyond our knowledge or of no real importance.

Following the world's patterns draws us away from Christ.

All the ceremonies of the old covenant were shadows.

Their true substance is found in Jesus Christ.

His complete sacrifice for sin and his revelation of God's will supply everything those outward observances could not provide.

To be complete in Christ means to possess everything necessary for salvation.

We are in him not merely when we look toward a distant Savior, but when the Holy Spirit creates faith in our hearts and joins us to Christ our Head.

Inward circumcision of the heart, putting sinful desires to death, dying and being buried to sin and the world, and rising to newness of life are realities portrayed in baptism and brought about through Spirit-given faith.

These show that God forgives sins and frees believers from the law's curse.

We were spiritually dead in sins, but Christ makes us alive.

His death is the death of our sins; his resurrection brings life to our souls.

Christ removed the ordinances that burdened Jewish believers and formed a dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles.

When the substance came, the shadows disappeared.

Every mortal human being is guilty under the written law's sentence of death.

How dreadful, then, the condition of those who scorn the Son of God's blood, through which alone that condemning record can be wiped away!

Do not be troubled by narrow, legalistic judgments concerning food, drink and Jewish festivals.

Setting aside time for God's worship and service is a moral obligation that does not change.

But the obligation is not inseparably tied to the seventh day of the week.

Christians keep the first day, the Lord's Day, in remembrance of his resurrection.

All Jewish ceremonies were shadows pointing toward the gospel's blessings.

Christ alone is our Mediator and Head (verses 18–23)

Appealing to angels for help can appear humble, as though people admitted they were too unworthy to speak directly to God.

But this is not permissible worship.

It gives a created being the honor belonging to Christ alone.

Such apparent humility is actually pride.

Worshiping angels means failing to honor Christ, the only Mediator between God and humanity.

To seek other spiritual intercessors is to insult the Lord, the Head of the church.

Those who release their hold on Christ grasp at things that cannot help them.

Christ's body, the church, is a growing body.

Genuine believers cannot live according to the world's fashions.

Wisdom means remaining close to the gospel's appointed means, entirely submitted to Jesus Christ, the church's only Head.

Self-imposed hardship and fasting can look like exceptional spirituality or willingness to suffer.

But practices invented by human preference do not honor God merely because they are difficult.

They actually gratify self-will, self-admiration, self-righteousness and contempt for others.

Their appearance of wisdom is extremely shallow, and they do not provide true spiritual benefit or overcome sinful desires.

Let us regard as morally indifferent whatever the Lord has left to individual freedom.

Grant other believers the same liberty.

Remember how quickly earthly things pass away, and use them to glorify God.
classic_reading:
[Col.2.1-Col.2.7]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The apostle expresses his love to, and joy in believers. | (1-7) |
He cautions against the errors of heathen philosophy; also against Jewish traditions, and rites which had been fulfilled in Christ. | (8-17) |
Against worshipping angels; and against legal ordinances. | (18-23) |
Verses 1-7
The soul prospers when we have clear knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus. When we not only believe with the heart, but are ready, when called, to make confession with the mouth. Knowledge and faith make a soul rich. The stronger our faith, and the warmer our love, the more will our comfort be. The treasures of wisdom are hid, not from us, but for us, in Christ. These were hid from proud unbelievers, but displayed in the person and redemption of Christ. See the danger of enticing words; how many are ruined by the false disguises and fair appearances of evil principles and wicked practices! Be aware and afraid of those who would entice to any evil; for they aim to spoil you. All Christians have, in profession at least, received Jesus Christ the Lord, consented to him, and taken him for theirs. We cannot be built up in Christ, or grow in him, unless we are first rooted in him, or founded upon him. Being established in the faith, we must abound therein, and improve in it more and more. God justly withdraws this benefit from those who do not receive it with thanksgiving; and gratitude for his mercies is justly required by God.
[Col.2.8-Col.2.17]
Verses 8-17
There is a philosophy which rightly exercises our reasonable faculties; a study of the works of God, which leads us to the knowledge of God, and confirms our faith in him. But there is a philosophy which is vain and deceitful; and while it pleases men's fancies, hinders their faith: such are curious speculations about things above us, or no concern to us. Those who walk in the way of the world, are turned from following Christ. We have in Him the substance of all the shadows of the ceremonial law. All the defects of it are made up in the gospel of Christ, by his complete sacrifice for sin, and by the revelation of the will of God. To be complete, is to be furnished with all things necessary for salvation. By this one word "complete," is shown that we have in Christ whatever is required. "In him," not when we look to Christ, as though he were distant from us, but we are in him, when, by the power of the Spirit, we have faith wrought in our hearts by the Spirit, and we are united to our Head. The circumcision of the heart, the crucifixion of the flesh, the death and burial to sin and to the world, and the resurrection to newness of life, set forth in baptism, and by faith wrought in our hearts, prove that our sins are forgiven, and that we are fully delivered from the curse of the law. Through Christ, we, who were dead in sins, are quickened. Christ's death was the death of our sins; Christ's resurrection is the quickening of our souls. The law of ordinances, which was a yoke to the Jews, and a partition-wall to the Gentiles, the Lord Jesus took out of the way. When the substance was come, the shadows fled. Since every mortal man is, through the hand-writing of the law, guilty of death, how very dreadful is the condition of the ungodly and unholy, who trample under foot that blood of the Son of God, whereby alone this deadly hand-writing can be blotted out! Let not any be troubled about bigoted judgments which related to meats, or the Jewish solemnities. The setting apart a portion of our time for the worship and service of God, is a moral and unchangeable duty, but had no necessary dependence upon the seventh day of the week, the sabbath of the Jews. The first day of the week, or the Lord's day, is the time kept holy by Christians, in remembrance of Christ's resurrection. All the Jewish rites were shadows of gospel blessings.
[Col.2.18-Col.2.23]
Verses 18-23
It looked like humility to apply to angels, as if men were conscious of their unworthiness to speak directly to God. But it is not warrantable; it is taking that honour which is due to Christ only, and giving it to a creature. There really was pride in this seeming humility. Those who worship angels, disclaim Christ, who is the only Mediator between God and man. It is an insult to Christ, who is the Head of the church, to use any intercessors but him. When men let go their hold of Christ, they catch at what will stand them in no stead. The body of Christ is a growing body. And true believers cannot live in the fashions of the world. True wisdom is, to keep close to the appointments of the gospel; in entire subjection to Christ, who is the only Head of his church. Self-imposed sufferings and fastings, might have a show of uncommon spirituality and willingness for suffering, but this was not "in any honour" to God. The whole tended, in a wrong manner, to satisfy the carnal mind, by gratifying self-will, self-wisdom, self-righteousness, and contempt of others. The things being such as carry not with them so much as the show of wisdom; or so faint a show that they do the soul no good, and provide not for the satisfying of the flesh. What the Lord has left indifferent, let us regard as such, and leave others to the like freedom; and remembering the passing nature of earthly things, let us seek to glorify God in the use of them.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Colossians exhorted to be heavenly-minded;1–4to mortify all corrupt affections;5–11to live in mutual love, forbearance, and forgiveness;12–17and to practise the duties of wives and husbands, children, parents, and servants.18–25
Seek what is above, where Christ reigns (verses 1–4)

Because Christians are free from the ceremonial requirements of the Mosaic law, they should pursue gospel obedience all the more carefully.

Heaven and earth pull our affections in different directions.

We cannot make both the chief purpose of our lives.

Love for the one weakens attachment to the other.

Regenerated people are dead to sin because its dominion has been broken through grace.

Its remaining power is gradually reduced as God's Spirit works in the soul.

At last, when believers are perfected in heavenly glory, sin's power will disappear completely.

To be dead in this sense means that the Holy Spirit enables us to put sinful desires to death, value earthly things less and long for heavenly blessings more.

We have not yet seen Jesus Christ with our own eyes.

But our comfort is that our life is secure with him.

The Holy Spirit brings the living water of Christ's grace into believers' souls through faith.

Christ lives within them by his Spirit, and they live for him in everything they do.

When Christ returns, all the redeemed will be gathered together.

Those whose lives are now hidden with him will appear with him in glory.

Since we look forward to such happiness, why should we set our deepest affections upon a world that passes away?

Put to death sinful desires and worldly greed (verses 5–11)

We must oppose the sinful habits and impulses that draw us toward the world's values.

Treat them like weeds or destructive pests that spread and ruin everything around them.

They must be put to death, restrained and continually resisted.

Make no provision for satisfying sinful desires.

Avoid situations that tempt us, including sensual indulgence, attachment to worldly pleasures and greed.

Greed is idolatry because it gives earthly things the love and devotion that belong to God.

Sin must be put to death because if we do not destroy it, it will destroy us.

The gospel transforms not only bodily desires but also the higher faculties of the mind and soul.

It strengthens the proper rule of reason and conscience over appetite and passion.

Country of origin, social position and the circumstances of life do not establish different standards of holiness.

Everyone is called to be holy.

For the Christian, Christ is all—the only Lord and Savior, the foundation of every hope and the source of all true happiness.

Clothe yourselves with compassion, forgiveness and gratitude (verses 12–17)

Christian duty includes more than avoiding harm.

We must do all the good we can for other people.

Those chosen and loved by God ought to be humble and compassionate toward everyone.

While sin remains in our hearts, disagreement and conflict may still occur.

But believers must forgive one another, imitating the forgiveness through which we ourselves have been saved.

Let God's peace rule in our hearts.

It is his own work among his people.

Thanksgiving to God helps make our character agreeable and useful to others.

The gospel is the word of Christ.

Many people possess that word but allow it to live within them only weakly. It has little authority over their lives.

Our souls flourish when we are filled with Scripture and the grace of Christ.

When we sing psalms, our hearts should feel the truths we sing, rather than merely pronounce words.

Whatever our occupation, perform everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, relying upon him with faith.

Those who do all things in his name will never lack reasons for gratitude to God the Father.

Serve Christ faithfully in every household relationship (verses 18–25)

The New Testament letters that most fully proclaim God's grace and the glory of Christ are also among those that explain our ordinary Christian responsibilities most carefully.

We must never separate gospel privileges from gospel duties.

Henry describes wives' duty as submission to their own husbands, not to cruel rulers or harsh tyrants.

Their husbands are bound to treat them with tender, faithful love.

Children who obey their parents are most likely to prosper.

Parents must likewise be gentle and compassionate, while children fulfill their duty of obedience.

Servants should obey their masters in everything consistent with their duty to God, their heavenly Master.

Their work must be just, honest and diligent, not driven by selfish calculation or outward pretense.

Believers who fear God remain faithful even when no human supervisor watches, because they know God sees their conduct.

They should work energetically rather than lazily, and cheerfully rather than resenting the position in which Providence has placed them.

Their encouragement is that through lawful and faithful service they serve Christ himself, who will reward them gloriously.

But those who do wrong will be held accountable for the wrong.

This applies equally to masters who treat servants unjustly.

The righteous Judge will judge both parties fairly.

Master and servant stand on the same level before his tribunal.

How much happier would the world be if genuine Christianity influenced every rank, relationship and condition of life!

But people who profess the gospel while neglecting duties and giving just grounds for complaint to those around them deceive themselves and bring disgrace upon Christ's message.
classic_reading:
[Col.3.1-Col.3.4]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The Colossians exhorted to be heavenly-minded;
(1-4)
to mortify all corrupt affections;
(5-11)
to live in mutual love, forbearance, and forgiveness;
(12-17)
and to practise the duties of wives and husbands, children, parents, and servants.
(18-25)
Verses 1-4
As Christians are freed from the ceremonial law, they must walk the more closely with God in gospel obedience. As heaven and earth are contrary one to the other, both cannot be followed together; and affection to the one will weaken and abate affection to the other. Those that are born again are dead to sin, because its dominion is broken, its power gradually subdued by the operation of grace, and it shall at length be extinguished by the perfection of glory. To be dead, then, means this, that those who have the Holy Spirit, mortifying within them the lusts of the flesh, are able to despise earthly things, and to desire those that are heavenly. Christ is, at present, one whom we have not seen; but our comfort is, that our life is safe with him. The streams of this living water flow into the soul by the influences of the Holy Spirit, through faith. Christ lives in the believer by his Spirit, and the believer lives to him in all he does. At the second coming of Christ, there will be a general assembling of all the redeemed; and those whose life is now hid with Christ, shall then appear with him in his glory. Do we look for such happiness, and should we not set our affections upon that world, and live above this?
[Col.3.5-Col.3.11]
Verses 5-11
It is our duty to mortify our members which incline to the things of the world. Mortify them, kill them, suppress them, as weeds or vermin which spread and destroy all about them. Continual opposition must be made to all corrupt workings, and no provision made for carnal indulgences. Occasions of sin must be avoided: the lusts of the flesh, and the love of the world; and covetousness, which is idolatry; love of present good, and of outward enjoyments. It is necessary to mortify sins, because if we do not kill them, they will kill us. The gospel changes the higher as well as the lower powers of the soul, and supports the rule of right reason and conscience, over appetite and passion. There is now no difference from country, or conditions and circumstances of life. It is the duty of every one to be holy, because Christ is a Christian's All, his only Lord and Saviour, and all his hope and happiness.
[Col.3.12-Col.3.17]
Verses 12-17
We must not only do no hurt to any, but do what good we can to all. Those who are the elect of God, holy and beloved, ought to be lowly and compassionate towards all. While in this world, where there is so much corruption in our hearts, quarrels will sometimes arise. But it is our duty to forgive one another, imitating the forgiveness through which we are saved. Let the peace of God rule in your hearts; it is of his working in all who are his. Thanksgiving to God, helps to make us agreeable to all men. The gospel is the word of Christ. Many have the word, but it dwells in them poorly; it has no power over them. The soul prospers, when we are full of the Scriptures and of the grace of Christ. But when we sing psalms, we must be affected with what we sing. Whatever we are employed about, let us do every thing in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in believing dependence on him. Those who do all in Christ's name, will never want matter of thanksgiving to God, even the Father.
[Col.3.18-Col.3.25]
Verses 18-25
The epistles most taken up in displaying the glory of the Divine grace, and magnifying the Lord Jesus, are the most particular in pressing the duties of the Christian life. We must never separate the privileges and duties of the gospel. Submission is the duty of wives. But it is submission, not to a severe lord or stern tyrant, but to her own husband, who is engaged to affectionate duty. And husbands must love their wives with tender and faithful affection. Dutiful children are the most likely to prosper. And parents must be tender, as well as children obedient. Servants are to do their duty, and obey their masters' commands, in all things consistent with duty to God their heavenly Master. They must be both just and diligent; without selfish designs, or hypocrisy and disguise. Those who fear God, will be just and faithful when from under their master's eye, because they know they are under the eye of God. And do all with diligence, not idly and slothfully; cheerfully, not discontented at the providence of God which put them in that relation. And for servants' encouragement, let them know, that in serving their masters according to the command of Christ, they serve Christ, and he will give them a glorious reward at last. But, on the other hand, he who doeth wrong, shall receive for the wrong which he hath done. God will punish the unjust, as well as reward the faithful servant; and the same if masters wrong their servants. For the righteous Judge of the earth will deal justly between master and servant. Both will stand upon a level at his tribunal. How happy would true religion make the world, if it every where prevailed, influenced every state of things, and every relation of life! But the profession of those persons who are regardless of duties, and give just cause for complaint to those they are connected with, deceives themselves, as well as brings reproach on the gospel.

Masters must treat servants justly (verse 1)

Paul continued addressing the obligations of masters toward their servants.

They must provide not only basic justice, but strict fairness and kindness.

Masters should treat those under their authority in the same manner they hope God will treat them.

Persevere in prayer and speak with gracious wisdom (verses 2–6)

No Christian duty can be performed rightly unless we continue in earnest prayer and remain alert with thanksgiving.

Believers should pray especially for their ministers.

They should also act rightly toward people who do not believe.

In every encounter with unbelievers, we ought to seek their good and commend the Christian faith by every appropriate means.

Use your time diligently.

Even when a Christian commits no obvious act of wrongdoing, simple carelessness may cause other people to develop lasting prejudice against the gospel.

Let all our conversation be wise and suited to the occasion.

The subject need not always be spiritual, but the conversation must always be conducted with Christian grace.

Even when discussing ordinary things, our manner should reflect the Lord we serve.

Grace is like salt seasoning our speech, keeping it from corruption.

It is not enough merely to answer another person's question.

We must answer truthfully, wisely and in an appropriate way.

Fellow servants share Christ's privileges (verses 7–9)

Gospel ministers serve Jesus Christ and are also fellow servants to one another.

They share one Lord, though he assigns different responsibilities and abilities to each.

Knowing that other believers care about us brings tremendous comfort when we face life's troubles.

Earthly position or circumstances make no difference to the spiritual relationship between sincere Christians.

They share the same gospel privileges and should receive the same respect and love.

See the wonderful change divine grace produces!

Previously unfaithful servants become faithful, beloved brothers, and people who once acted wrongly become trustworthy partners in doing good.

Paul commends faithful coworkers and ends with grace (verses 10–18)

Paul had once disagreed seriously with Barnabas over Mark.

But now he was not merely reconciled with Mark—he recommended him to the churches.

What an example of Christian forgiveness!

When someone has sincerely turned from a fault, we should not hold it against that person forever.

We must forget as well as forgive.

Paul drew strength and encouragement from the fellowship of saints and gospel ministers.

Some were fellow servants, others fellow prisoners, and all shared in working out their own salvation while seeking the salvation of other people.

Earnest, effective prayer has great power.

Yet some who are called to ministry fall short of their responsibilities.

Worldly praise or criticism, the influence of false teaching or selfish ambition can draw them into preaching and living in ways that fail to fulfill their calling.

But those who proclaim the same gospel Paul preached and follow his example may expect God's favor and blessing.
classic_reading:
[Col.4.1]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Masters to do their duty towards servants. | (1) |
Persons of all ranks to persevere in prayer, and Christian prudence. | (2-6) |
The apostle refers to others for an account of his affairs. | (7-9) |
Sends greetings; and concludes with a blessing. | (10-18) |
Verse 1
The apostle proceeds with the duty of masters to their servants. Not only justice is required of them, but strict equity and kindness. Let them deal with servants as they expect God should deal with themselves.
[Col.4.2-Col.4.6]
Verses 2-6
No duties can be done aright, unless we persevere in fervent prayer, and watch therein with thanksgiving. The people are to pray particularly for their ministers. Believers are exhorted to right conduct towards unbelievers. Be careful in all converse with them, to do them good, and recommend religion by all fit means. Diligence in redeeming time, commends religion to the good opinion of others. Even what is only carelessness may cause a lasting prejudice against the truth. Let all discourse be discreet and seasonable, as becomes Christians. Though it be not always of grace, it must always be with grace. Though our discourse be of that which is common, yet it must be in a Christian manner. Grace is the salt which seasons our discourse, and keeps it from corrupting. It is not enough to answer what is asked, unless we answer aright also.
[Col.4.7-Col.4.9]
Verses 7-9
Ministers are servants to Christ, and fellow-servants to one another. They have one Lord, though they have different stations and powers for service. It is a great comfort under the troubles and difficulties of life, to have fellow Christians caring for us. Circumstances of life make no difference in the spiritual relation among sincere Christians; they partake of the same privileges, and are entitled to the same regards. What amazing changes Divine grace makes! Faithless servants become faithful and beloved brethren, and some who had done wrong, become fellow-workers of good.
[Col.4.10-Col.4.18]
Verses 10-18
Paul had differed with Barnabas, on the account of this Mark, yet he is not only reconciled, but recommends him to the churches; an example of a truly Christian and forgiving spirit. If men have been guilty of a fault, it must not always be remembered against them. We must forget as well as forgive. The apostle had comfort in the communion of saints and ministers. One is his fellow-servant, another his fellow-prisoner, and all his fellow-workers, working out their own salvation, and endeavouring to promote the salvation of others. The effectual, fervent prayer is the prevailing prayer, and availeth much. The smiles, flatteries, or frowns of the world, the spirit of error, or the working of self-love, leads many to a way of preaching and living which comes far short of fulfilling their ministry. But those who preach the same doctrine as Paul, and follow his example, may expect the Divine favour and blessing.
